about: Every competitor is dealt one card: an ECC agent chain (which Everything-Claude-Code agents it works as, in order), a reasoning mode, a strategy, and an emphasis lens it obsesses over. Emphasis and chain are dealt round-robin so that with 12 or more competitors every emphasis is covered at least once. No two competitors get the same card.

chains.name: Planner, architect, TDD guide, code reviewer
chains.how: Plan the phases first, design the system second, define the tests third, then review the whole as a hostile reviewer would.

chains.name: Architect, security reviewer, database reviewer
chains.how: Design from the threat model and the data model outward. Every component must say how it fails safely and what it stores.

chains.name: GAN planner, marketing agent, a11y architect
chains.how: Write the product spec as if for a launch: audience, features, sprints, acceptance criteria, how it is sold, who it excludes.

chains.name: Loop operator, performance optimizer, doc updater
chains.how: Start from day-two operations: deploys, monitoring, cost, runbooks, documentation. Design the product so it can be run by someone who did not build it.

chains.name: Spec miner, TDD guide, PR test analyzer
chains.how: Write the requirements as testable specs with invariants first. Every feature gets its acceptance test before its design.

chains.name: Code explorer, code architect, refactor cleaner
chains.how: Map what exists or what the closest existing systems do, then produce an implementation blueprint with concrete files, interfaces and build order, and cut everything not needed.

chains.name: Security reviewer, silent failure hunter, type design analyzer
chains.how: Assume every input is hostile and every dependency will fail. Design the types so illegal states cannot be represented, and make every failure loud.

chains.name: TypeScript reviewer, React reviewer, database reviewer, e2e runner
chains.how: Design the web product through the eyes of the four reviewers who will tear it apart: the frontend, the backend types, the queries and the end-to-end flows.

chains.name: Planner, Python reviewer, FastAPI reviewer, database reviewer
chains.how: Design a Python service: API contracts, schemas, async boundaries and the database behind them, with the review rules of each reviewer applied up front.

chains.name: Architect, Go reviewer, Rust reviewer
chains.how: Design as a systems engineer: explicit concurrency, ownership of every resource, explicit error paths, no hidden allocation of trust.

chains.name: Swift reviewer, Kotlin reviewer, Flutter reviewer, a11y architect
chains.how: Design for a phone in a pocket first: offline, interrupted, one-handed, notifications, app store rules. The web is the second client.

chains.name: MLE reviewer, RAG pipeline reviewer, database reviewer
chains.how: Treat every decision the product makes as a model with inputs, evaluation and drift. Specify data contracts, evaluation and rollback for each.

chains.name: Opensource forker, sanitizer, packager
chains.how: Design it as something strangers will run and contribute to: licenses, secrets hygiene, setup in one command, contribution rules, no internal references.

chains.name: Harness optimizer, agent evaluator, GAN evaluator
chains.how: Write the evaluation before the product: what will be measured, how pass and fail are decided, and how the system proves it works every release.

reasoning.name: First principles
reasoning.how: Reduce the task to facts nobody can dispute, then rebuild from those. Keep a convention only when it earns its place again.

reasoning.name: Pre-mortem
reasoning.how: Assume the project shipped and failed badly a year later. Write the post-mortem, then design so that each cause cannot happen.

reasoning.name: Inversion
reasoning.how: List every way to guarantee the project fails, then design the opposite of each item.

reasoning.name: Analogy to proven systems
reasoning.how: Find the three closest systems that already work in the world and borrow their hard-won rules, saying which rule came from where.

reasoning.name: Adversarial
reasoning.how: Play the fraudster, the lawyer, the angry customer, the tired operator and the bored moderator in turn, and design against each.

reasoning.name: Constraints first
reasoning.how: Write every hard constraint (law, money, time, platform, physics) before any feature. Features must fit inside the constraints, never the reverse.

reasoning.name: User journey
reasoning.how: Walk one real person through the product minute by minute from first contact to leaving, and design whatever that walk needs.

reasoning.name: State machines
reasoning.how: Model every important thing as explicit states and transitions, name the illegal transitions, and design around them.

reasoning.name: Follow the money
reasoning.how: Trace every unit of value from where it enters to where it leaves, including fees, refunds, limits, taxes and who is liable at each step.

reasoning.name: Decision ledger
reasoning.how: For every decision write the options, the one chosen and why, so a reader can disagree with a specific line rather than the whole.

reasoning.name: Minimum then expand
reasoning.how: Define the smallest version that is complete, legal and safe, then list what the next three versions add and why.

reasoning.name: Reference class forecasting
reasoning.how: Estimate cost, time and risk from what comparable projects actually took, and say which comparables you used.

strategies.name: Simplest thing that works
strategies.how: Choose the least complicated design that fully does the job. Every extra part must justify itself.

strategies.name: Boring technology
strategies.how: Pick managed, mainstream, well-documented pieces. Novelty only where the product is the novelty.

strategies.name: Safety first
strategies.how: When a trade-off touches money, law, data or users' trust, pick the safer side every time and say what it costs.

strategies.name: Fastest credible launch
strategies.how: Optimize for a real launch soon. Cut scope aggressively, but never cut what makes it legal or safe.

strategies.name: Ready for ten times the load
strategies.how: Design so the first version survives a ten-times spike without a rewrite, and say exactly where it would break at a hundred times.

strategies.name: Operator friendly
strategies.how: Prefer designs that a small team can run, debug and explain at three in the morning.

strategies.name: Every rule written down
strategies.how: Every limit, threshold, fee, timeout and eligibility rule gets a number, an owner and a reason. Nothing is left as 'configurable later'.

strategies.name: Defensive by default
strategies.how: Assume abuse, outages and mistakes. Every feature says how it is limited, monitored and reversed.

strategies.name: Earn trust visibly
strategies.how: Make every rule that affects the user visible to them before it applies, and make every outcome explainable after.

strategies.name: Composable modules
strategies.how: Split the system into modules with explicit contracts so any one can be replaced without touching the rest.

strategies.name: Measure everything that matters
strategies.how: Every feature ships with its metric, its alert and the decision that metric will drive.

strategies.name: Regulated grade
strategies.how: Design as if an auditor will read it: audit trails, retention, separation of duties, documented controls.

emphasis.name: Legal and compliance
emphasis.how: Obsess over jurisdiction, licenses, terms, privacy, consumer and financial regulation, and what gets the project shut down.

emphasis.name: Money, limits and fraud
emphasis.how: Obsess over every amount: pricing, spend limits, caps, quotas, fees, refunds, reconciliation, fraud and chargebacks. Every limit needs a number.

emphasis.name: Rules, voting and disputes
emphasis.how: Obsess over how decisions are made inside the product: voting mechanics, eligibility, weighting, ties, changing votes, sybil resistance, disputes and appeals.

emphasis.name: Identity, roles and permissions
emphasis.how: Obsess over who can do what, how they prove who they are, how access is revoked, and how every privileged action is logged.

emphasis.name: Data model and lifecycle
emphasis.how: Obsess over the data: model, ownership, retention, deletion, export, backups, migrations and personal data.

emphasis.name: Core logic and edge cases
emphasis.how: Obsess over states, transitions, concurrency, time zones, idempotency, limits, empty states and the inputs nobody expects.

emphasis.name: Security and abuse
emphasis.how: Obsess over the threat model, abuse vectors, rate limits, secrets, injection, bots and reporting.

emphasis.name: Reliability and operations
emphasis.how: Obsess over failure modes, monitoring, deploys, rollback, incidents, runbooks, performance and the cost of running it.

emphasis.name: Logistics and the real world
emphasis.how: Obsess over everything outside the software: physical flows, scheduling, third parties, vendors, SLAs, geography, support and what happens when a dependency is down.

emphasis.name: User experience and communication
emphasis.how: Obsess over the flows, notifications, error messages, onboarding, mobile, offline, accessibility and every word the user reads.

emphasis.name: Testing and quality
emphasis.how: Obsess over acceptance criteria, the test plan, fixtures, how quality is proven every release, and the documentation that lets someone else take over.

emphasis.name: Delivery, scope and risk
emphasis.how: Obsess over purpose, non-goals, phases, milestones, team, timeline, cost, risks and open questions. Say what is version one and what is not.
